---
title: "Intraclass correlation"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

We have just shown that a [shared participant intercept](random-intercepts.qmd) enters every response from that participant. The [**intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat502/Lesson06) asks what proportion of their total modeled variation comes from that shared source. Recall that correlation divides covariance by the product of two standard deviations. When the two rows have the same marginal variance, that denominator is simply the common total variance.

The formal definitions of [variance and covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) supply that ratio. [Group deviations](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) supply the shared source, and conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) states what remains after those deviations are known. The [residual](residuals.qmd) is the observed response for a trial minus its fitted value. In ordinary language, the ICC is available because multiple lexical decision trials involve the same listener or spoken word.

We now derive that calculation, substitute the MALD variance estimates, and connect each ICC to the design's replication structure.

## Deriving the crossed-unit correlations

For the MALD intercept-only model,

$$
Y_{pwi}=\beta_0+b_p+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi},
$$

with independent components having variances $\tau_p^2$, $\tau_w^2$, and $\sigma^2$. The marginal response variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pwi}]
=\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2.
$$

Two distinct trials from the same participant but different words share only $b_p$, so their covariance is $\tau_p^2$. Their correlation is

$$
\rho_p
=\frac{\tau_p^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}.
$$

Two trials on the same word from different participants instead have

$$
\rho_w
=\frac{\tau_w^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}.
$$

If two rows share both participant and word, the fitted correlation is

$$
\rho_{pw}
=\frac{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}
=\rho_p+\rho_w.
$$

These expressions already show the comparison that matters. A same-participant pair shares the participant component, a same-word pair shares the word component, and a pair sharing both receives both covariance contributions. The next section substitutes estimates from the observed MALD responses rather than introducing an unrelated numerical illustration.

## Substituting the MALD variance estimates

```{r}
#| label: mald-icc
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ 1 +
    (1 | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

variance_table <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit))
participant_variance <- variance_table$vcov[
  variance_table$grp == "participant_id" & is.na(variance_table$var2)
]
item_variance <- variance_table$vcov[
  variance_table$grp == "item" & is.na(variance_table$var2)
]
residual_variance <- sigma(fit)^2
total_variance <- participant_variance + item_variance + residual_variance

icc <- data.frame(
  shared_unit = c("Participant", "Word item", "Participant and word"),
  covariance = c(
    participant_variance,
    item_variance,
    participant_variance + item_variance
  )
)
icc$correlation <- icc$covariance / total_variance
icc

variance_shares <- data.frame(
  source = c("Participant intercept", "Word intercept", "Trial residual"),
  fitted_variance = c(
    participant_variance,
    item_variance,
    residual_variance
  )
)
variance_shares$share_of_total <-
  variance_shares$fitted_variance / total_variance
variance_shares
```

The fitted participant ICC is `r sprintf("%.4f", icc$correlation[icc$shared_unit == "Participant"])`, the item ICC is `r sprintf("%.4f", icc$correlation[icc$shared_unit == "Word item"])`, and sharing both units gives correlation `r sprintf("%.4f", icc$correlation[icc$shared_unit == "Participant and word"])`. These values are computed from the correct-response MALD subset rather than supplied as schematic quantities.

The second table shows why each numerator must name its unit. The participant ICC uses the participant share of total variance; the word ICC uses the word share. The residual share remains in both denominators because each response contains trial variation even when two rows share a participant or word.

## Relating the correlations to replication

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-icc-repetition
repetition_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    unit = "Participant",
    repetitions = as.numeric(table(mald$participant_id))
  ),
  data.frame(
    unit = "Word item",
    repetitions = as.numeric(table(mald$item))
  )
)

ggplot(repetition_data, aes(x = repetitions)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey55", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~unit, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Correct trials per unit", y = "Units") +
  theme_classic()
```

Positive ICCs mean that repeated rows from one unit contain less independent information than the same number of rows from distinct units. Additional trials can estimate an observed participant's or word's baseline more precisely. Additional participants or words provide replication across the corresponding population.

There is no single crossed-design design effect analogous to $1+(m-1)\rho$ unless the cluster structure is simple and balanced. MALD rows can share a participant, a word, both, or neither, and the numbers of repetitions vary across both units.

## Keeping the interpretation model-specific

Adding predictors can change every variance component. An intercept-only ICC and an ICC conditional on frequency, duration, and trial order need not agree. Random slopes also make the covariance depend on predictor values, so one constant ICC no longer describes every trial pair. Logistic and Poisson mixed models require further scale choices because they do not estimate a Gaussian residual variance on the response scale.

These ICCs are properties of this fitted Gaussian intercept-only model and its correct-response subset. Report the formula and variance components with the ratios.

## Recap and check

1. Is the participant ICC the fraction of variance due to every repeated unit? No. Its numerator contains only participant-intercept variance.
2. Why can we not obtain an ICC for a logistic model by copying this denominator? A Bernoulli GLMM has no estimated Gaussian residual variance on the response scale; one must declare whether the ICC is defined on a latent or response scale.
